utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Registrar, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, distinguished gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to the members of the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the gentlemen from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones we represent the Defence for Mr. Naser Oric. We have our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you ask your teams. Any preliminaries? I notice -- yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Just one matter. I wanted to state for the record that we presented, or turned over some medical records that will be using today to the Defence last evening. We turned them over as soon as we received English translation. And with respect to another matter, yesterday, as the witness testified, we -- the Court permitted him to use a list that he prepared, and I think at this point we need to put an exhibit number to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, we would like an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll do that first and foremost. That will be Exhibit 474?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit 475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 475. Just for your information, before we rose, I asked the registrar to liaise with everyone to see how we could make adjustments to today's timetable, and the suggestion is, and I have been told that it meets with the approval of everyone, more or less, the suggestion is that we have a break at 11.00, and that will be a 30-minute break, then we start again at 11.30, and we go on until 1.00, maximum quarter past one, depending on where we are at the time. It will, of course, not curtail on the time you need with this witness for your cross-examination. So if need be, we'll go on until tomorrow. All right? Do you have any reservations, any comments, on this proposed schedule? No, all right. We can work on it, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. I hope you had a good rest yesterday afternoon and last night. We will be proceeding with the questions today, with the examination-in-chief, to be followed later on today by the cross-examination. I am not that sure that we will finish today. But if we don't finish today, we will certainly finish tomorrow. Yes, Ms. Richardson. You're still testifying under oath. I mean, I need hardly remind you of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yesterday, when we ended the court session yesterday, you testified that you had visited -- you were taken for questioning before a man who appeared to you to be a soldier, and that you were escorted by two soldiers. I would like to ask you at this point: Who did you believe this man to be?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I thought it was -- this man was a judge, because I was escorted to this man by two soldiers and he was interrogating me. First of all, he asked me whether or not I knew a man by the name of Leskovac, and I still say, as I did then, that I do not know these men because I spent a lot of my time working in Belgrade and abroad and many people were unfamiliar to me, including some of my neighbours. I, for instance, didn't know their names. And, indeed, this was true for the men he inquired after.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you he was a judge?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And after seeing this man, were you and the other prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were. I've already said that here in the courtroom, that while he was interrogating me, he said that he was going to skin me and put salt in my wounds. And upon my return to the cell, the beatings resumed as before, with metal rods, with rifle butts, wooden staffs, bats, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the area of your testimony where you stated that there were prisoners brought in from Cerska.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And those prisoners were Branko Sekulic, Jakov Djukic, Dragan Ilic, and Rade Pejic. There was also a female called Andza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Did you have an opportunity to speak with these prisoners when they were brought in?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have much occasion to talk to these prisoners. It was only in those intervals when we were conscious, and this usually happened in the early morning hours. And the person who could speak most of the time was Ratko Nikolic, because he was awake, and then he would ask others like, for instance, "Ilija, are you alive," along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Did the prisoners from Cerska appear to have been beaten prior to arriving at the national defence building in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These prisoners were telling us what had happened to them, and I learnt of this later on at the hospital, that they had been beaten, that they slept -- they had slept in one of the barns, and then they would bring them acorns to eat. He said that at the time that they wished many times to simply die. They had also apparently tried to bake the soles of the shoes on a makeshift stove because they really had nothing else to eat. According to their story, a woman who was from the area would bring them plums, and this would constitute the greatest of joys for them. She was consoling them, she was a balm to their soul, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: After they arrived at Srebrenica and were put into the cell with you and the others, did they -- were they beaten on a daily basis, as yourself and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Upon their arrival to the cell, the mistreatment and beatings resumed, just as I've described earlier on, but I can repeat, with rods, bats, rifle butts. What I found hardest to bear was that when this Stanko, called Cane, had to go out to the toilet, he, unaware of whether these people were around, he was basically unaware of anyone around him. He apparently set out and then thought he was going home. The soldiers who were there, around, would then beat him. He was a disabled man; his hand and his legs were disabled. And they would target those limbs exactly, and would beat him with whatever they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident, or more than one incident, with respect to the other prisoner, Rade Pejic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Rade Pejic, I can say the following, I don't know if I've already said this: This was in the reception room when Dzemo Tihic approached him and set his beard on fire. First, actually, he said, "Look at this Chetnik, he doesn't want to shave off his beard." And the man retorted, "How can I shave myself? I have nothing to shave myself with." And then this Dzemo Tihic set his beard on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What happened after?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, one of the soldiers - at the time the beard was still sizzling - this other man said, "What will that other man say about this?" And he tried to put out the fire. However, the victim himself didn't dare to put the fire out, because whenever we winced or shirked as they were beating us, then they would just start beating us more and say, "Look, he's trying to put up resistance."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this Tihic, was he a soldier or was he a guard? Or how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just finish this story about Rade Pejic. After they had set this man's beard on fire, they forced us to lie down on the floor, beat us, and that was when they broke my cheekbone. And this was the first time that they broke my nose. Rade Pejic -- that is, the soldier who was also in this room, wanted to push Rade's head into this makeshift stove that was there. Luckily, the other soldier that was there prevented him from doing so. And he called him names and told him again, "What will he" - with a capital "H" - "say if he hears of this?"

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you know who "he" was, who that reference was to?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Dzemo Tihic. And I know him well because I would always pass by his house when I was walking through my village that I grew up in. He wasn't the only one to beat us. There were several other soldiers. Whoever wanted to could beat us. But it's very difficult for me to recall. It was dark. And it was him that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how was he, Tihic, dressed? Was he in uniform or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Pejic? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, the person who -- I'll repeat the question. The person who set fire to Pejic's beard, to Rade Pejic's beard.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person was wearing a camouflage uniform. And I repeat: This was the man that I knew well, unlike the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is something that I am unable to follow. Let's go back to page 6, line 23, when he starts -- line 21. You asked him: "And this Tihic, was he a soldier or was he a guard? Or how was he dressed?" And then he answers: "Let me just finish the story about Rade Pejic. After they had set this man's beard on fire, they forced us to lie down on the floor, beat us, and that was when they broke my cheekbone. And this was the first time when they broke my nose. Rade Pejic - that is, the soldier - was also in this room and wanted to push Rade's head into the makeshift stove. That was -- luckily, the other soldier that was there prevented him from doing so. And he called him names and told him, 'what will he' - with a capital 'H' - 'say if he hears of this.'" And then you put the question: "Did you know who he was, who that reference was to?" And his answer is: "Yes, that's right. Dzemo Tihic. And I know him well, because I would always pass by his house when I was walking through my village that I grew up in. He wasn't the only one to beat us. There were --" it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can go back. I actually intended to do that, to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, when you testified that a soldier put out -- a soldier managed to -- let me rephrase. You mentioned that the person you knew before -- that you knew before, Dzemo Tihic, set fire to Rade's beard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And then a soldier, Rade -- excuse me, someone else, a soldier, managed to put out the fire that was set to Rade's beard; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And now, you also mentioned that there was an incident with the furnace where this same person that you knew from before, Tihic, Dzemo Tihic, attempted to put Rade's head into a furnace.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And then I think you mentioned it was someone else there who prevented or took out Rade's head from the furnace.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you testified that someone said, I believe you said the person who pulled out Rade's head, said "What would he say?"

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Who was the "he" that this person made reference to?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. But you said "he," "what would he say?" Who was "he"? Who did you think that they were referring to? Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I remember that they kept using this term "he," "the boss," or "Naser." At that particular point I didn't know who he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the incident where Rade's beard was set on fire and his head was put in the furnace, did this happen on two separate occasions or did this happen on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion. It was on that same night, when we were taken out to the reception room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that any of the prisoners died during the time that you were held in the national defence building?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the All People's Defence building, and this is stated in the report that I made, Kojo, nicknamed Kosta -- rather, Kosta, nicknamed Kojo, was the first one to die. Apparently he was from Bratunac. And he died as a result of severe beatings. That same night, it was perhaps in the early morning hours, soldiers came with a military blanket, and they wrote something down own a piece of paper - I couldn't say what they wrote down - put this piece of paper in his pocket and took him away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Had he been beaten that day, before he died; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on a regular basis. There's no need to keep repeating this. Whenever anybody willed to beat someone, they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When did you first become aware that Kosta had died?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One morning, before they started beating us again, Ratko Nikolic yelled, "Ilija, Ilija." I was still half asleep, but I yelled back. "Do you know that Kosta has died?" I was stunned by this. And then after all of this, those people who brought him in in the first place came and took him away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did any of those prisoners inform the guards or anyone else that Kosta had died?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, it was in the morning, I don't remember the exact time. They came in through the prisoners' door. There were two persons. They wrote something down on a slip of paper, placed it on the cell, and left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this Kosta that you're referring to, is that Kostadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kosta, Kojo, that's how I remember him, and that's all I know about him. And I'm trying to keep it that way in my mind. I have no particular desire to remember his last name or anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that someone else, one of the other prisoners, died?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't give you the exact time - it was, perhaps, a day or two later - Mico from Sase died. The next day, probably the next day, he was beaten by a young man in the chest. He probably began bleeding inside his lungs when he was beaten like that. But a while after he started talking to himself. "Dragan, my son, bring me water."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when did he die? How soon after he started speaking -- talking to himself?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about that. I can't remember exactly what I said at the time. I simply wasn't able to remember, even then. It was perhaps two days later, that's if memory serves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And when did you first become aware that he had died?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same thing throughout. Ratko was the most conscious one of us, and he used to say things. It was the same thing throughout, all over again. The same two people came. They would write something down on a slip of paper and put it on the blanket. And then where they took the blanket, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know what they wrote on the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I have no idea. I wasn't able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned -- you testified yesterday that Svetlana Trifunovic was at the prison. Did you see any other Serb children at the prison while you were held there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Branko. Branko would also sometimes appear at the same door. I heard him playing up and down the corridor. I have no idea who his playmates were. I never heard that they were beating him. Branko, on the other hand, never came into our cell to spit at us, like Svetlana used to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when men and women were exchanged, men and women prisoners, that is?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After a certain time, it was halfway through my stay there, the women were exchanged. Mile Trifunovic was exchanged along with them, as well as Cane and Miloje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall if Branko was also exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko? Yes, yes, most probably. He was in our prison, but I assumed that he had also left and joined the women on the way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would like to have the clip of Prosecution Exhibit -- I believe it's 446.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's already on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, please turn your attention to the screen in front of you, and we will play this clip for you. And as we're going through the clip, please let us know if there is anything that you recognise in the clip.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is the police station, what I just saw in the previous frame. This is the road leading from the police station to the town hall. This is the police station, as far as I can tell. The entrance. To the right you can see the room in which I was lying. You take this corridor. I need to have a good look, I need to remember. It was nighttime, after all, at the time, and I need to remember the corridor. This is outside -- this is just inside the entrance, and outside the reception room, this is a flight of stairs leading up to the first floor. At the far end of this corridor, you see a door leading to the cell in which I was detained. Right, these are the bars that I spoke about, a radiator and a window. Well, you can see inside the cell. This was not there at the time. I'm not sure when this footage was taken. This is the corridor. It's very difficult for me to tell exactly, if I only look at this footage of the room itself. When I was brought in, it was nighttime, and I was less alive than dead, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. But does the -- I understand that you stated that something -- the items that you saw in the room, in the cell, was not present. Does this footage seem familiar to you in that the structure itself --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Does the structure, the rooms and its location, appear familiar?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent that I remember. It was nighttime, after all, when I was brought in. I did draw that sketch for you, and I think the sketch reflects what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I'd ask that you continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And again, as it's playing, let us know if there is anything that seems familiar to you. Here's another clip.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the street leading to the town hall and the department store. This is where my clothes were taken away. If you can just veer slightly to the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we're sort of confined to this particular video. But if you see a building that you recognise, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we are. Yes, this is exactly what I'm talking about, where this person is standing, outside that door, or thereabouts. I think this is the building where my clothes were taken away, my boots, my watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Is it the building to your right or to your left that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one on the left. This man, who is facing me, or rather the police station, is standing just outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It appears to be a white building, from the video clip. All right. If you can continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There's another clip.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the town hall. I was taken to the town hall to see that man who then interrogated me. This is an alleyway down which I was taken to the cell. To the left you can see the court building. I believe my description was actually quite accurate. Between the court and the town hall, there was a flight of concrete steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Before we continue the clip, when you were interrogated by the man at the town hall building, were you taken with -- did this happen on the first floor, or were you taken upstairs someplace?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this a number of times already, but I can't remember. I know that that was where it happened. But whether we went up a flight of stairs or not, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right, that's fine. We'll let the video continue.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the court building. Again, we're going back to the same alley between the court and the town hall, down which I was taken to my cell. From here you can see the window of the room where they tried to stop up the breakage in the glass pane to keep us from suffocating. To the left is the entrance to the building. The entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We have another clip.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the one. These are probably some of the rooms inside the building. I'm not very clear about this. You can't expect me to identify a room if you have footage that was taken inside the room. If you had gone successively from the entrance and then went on down the corridor, perhaps I'd be better able to tell. Now, this is the room in which I was. I recognise the pipes behind the table. Not this one, the previous one. I really can't form a mental image now. Yes, yes, this one, this room. That's where the arrow is pointing. This is probably the room to which we were taken. It's difficult for me to say just by looking at this. I was quite taken aback, and I was bleeding profusely. I was not able to observe in detail. Again, the room straight down the corridor, to the right there was a lavatory, and outside the lavatory was a reception room into which I was taken. There were bars on the window of that room. I think I always said I didn't know whether there were two or three windows. I didn't keep track at the time. What I see in the footage is certainly inside that building, but this is not the way I remember it. And the lavatory is all messed up, and this is not the way I remember it, if indeed this is the lavatory. The bench and the beds were not there. You can see the valves that I told you about, you can see them in this piece of footage. There was a cable that I pulled out of my underwear and placed under the linoleum in case they tried to cut me up so I could hang myself. But none of this was actually inside the room, so it's very difficult for me to recognise. But I do hope that I was able to notice some things. There were no beds inside the room by any means, that's for sure, or the blankets. If we'd had this back then, it would have seemed more like a hotel, probably. These are the windows with bars that I told you about through which the pipe of a makeshift stove was leaving the room. These two pipes are my reference points, because I used them as reference points every time I told this story. This wasn't like that. There's a cable that was torn out of the wall. This is not something I noticed at the time. It's very difficult for me to describe everything the way I did on my own piece of paper. If I look at it like this, this looks demolished. I have no idea when this footage was taken. It's very difficult for me to tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. So from your testimony, it appears that the video footage itself reflects a structure that is -- that appears to be damaged, or at the time you were held prisoner, the building itself was in a better condition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in a better condition. I explained about the access to that building and where I was inside the building. But if you look at the room, I'm absolutely certain anyone would be hard put to explain, especially the way I see it here in this frame. I told you that the building had some sort of a concrete floor or linoleum on which we slept. There was a table with two or three chairs in that room and a stove, which probably kept us from dying on account of the smoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So other than the structural damage that you see in the video that was not there at the time, the layout of the building itself appears familiar to you, as it did when you were held prisoner?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Yes. Yes, that's what I said, isn't it? But if you show me the room itself, it's difficult for me to remember. I do recognise the windows clearly, though. There were no panes on the windows.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here, the staff, I didn't see that at the time. But here you have all the rooms, I see them all in front of me now. The reception room, the lavatory, all the way down to our cell. That should be sufficient. That would be the room, the way I see it now. There were no beds. We were in a circle to the right. And then under these pipes there was a table with three chairs. Mico Trifunovic was seated in one of these.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this is the room where you were beaten daily?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult for me. Again, I'm telling you, I'm not sure if it was like this, or maybe we were just beaten so badly. I can explain to you exactly which way I got in, at least I remember that well, when I was being brought back from the town hall. And I remember that quite clearly. The room in which the women were kept is another thing that I remember. Two soldiers forced me and Ratko Nikolic to go and fetch some firewood. The room next to ours was empty, and the next room on the left was their room. If you -- well, I think I could tell you on the way out, down the corridor, I can tell you where the door was, but I was not even allowed to have a look, to look around and see if anyone was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. This video is almost completed. Do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. On the way out, I remember that one door. And because we couldn't just look; you walked with your head down. I've explained everything that I can. Yes. That's what the building looks like, the building towards which I was walking between the court and the town hall. This very window, the one that is singed, I think that is where the stove was. That's the entrance. This is the open space outside the building in which I was kept. That's the court building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. We can complete the video clip at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, next the Prosecution would like to show photographs to the witness, and I believe they were previously tendered. And that is Prosecution Exhibit 419.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, we have some images before you on the screen. If you would take a look, and tell us if you can identify what you see before you. If you can't, that's fine. Does this image look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson. For the record, what the witness is being shown is a photograph with ERN 03617694.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's not P419, at least not according to my records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I do have them here. It is 419? Yes, the first photo of 419.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For 419, I have ERN 03617712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we check, registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It could be that it's one picture of that bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is part of a range, so it could be that that's what Mr. Jones is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They were filed in more than one batch, Mr. Jones, and this is probably what is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have it now. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But in my records at least, and I invite Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser to check as well, in my records, this is as it is, in other words, P419, and this is the first photo in the series. And it does, indeed, have the ERN that I mentioned or I referred to earlier, for the record. All right? Shall we proceed? Okay, thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can put the question again to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, the image before you on the screen, do you recognise where that location and what that structure --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I see it now, I can't really say. I can't find my bearings here. As I've already told you, I haven't been to Srebrenica that often to be able to recognise every single building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. If you don't recognise it, you don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain things if I see them from a bit far off. But if I see a room with four walls, it's not really possible for me to recognise the location. But I think I've explained it quite well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please look at the next photograph. If you can't recognise it, that's fine, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is now being shown photo bearing ERN 03617696.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, at least judging by what I can see here. I just see the front of the building with the one or two windows, so I can't really ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's ERN 03617698.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This might be the cell that I was in. But just by seeing a radiator and this broken sink, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this photograph is ERN 03617700.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the next photograph is ERN 03617702. Do you recognise that image?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This reminds me of the room that the women were held in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. 03617704.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the room I was held in. I've said this already. I remember these valves very well, that there was -- to the right there was the lavatory and the reception room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. The next photograph, 03617706.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the front entrance to the building, as far as I can see, and this is where you can see the cell that we were in.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also the lobby, just after the entrance-way. This is the patch of the road between the court building and the cell we were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: ERN number 03617712. And the next photograph is 03617714.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you can see the corner of the building of the SUP and the municipality building, or rather, no, no, you can see the court, and then just in front of the court building, there's the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the next photograph, 03617716.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're interested in the building on the right-hand side, that's the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And this photograph, 03617718.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the corridor leading to the cell in the SUP, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the police station.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of this corridor, to the right there is the cell that I was held in at the S-U-P, SUP.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the SUP building as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: 03617728. This is the last photograph.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. Did there come a time that you were removed from the national defence building, where you were held, and taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to the hospital just prior to my exchange, and as far as I remember, that was the only time I had been at the hospital. I don't know how long I was kept there, perhaps for some five, six days, or maybe even longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were -- well, let's just go back for a moment. Do you remember how -- or who took you from the prison to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was Mandza and maybe two more soldiers, or maybe even more, on my way from the prison to the hospital. But I did not keep track of that, really. As they -- as we left the prison, although I don't remember this part very well, I believe we passed that stretch between the court and the municipality buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you the only prisoner taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was taken to the hospital together with Branko Sekulic and Rade Pejic. Upon our arrival there, we found Milomir Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the other prisoners remained in the prison, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the other prisoners who remained were Jakov Djukic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know if Dragan Ilic remained as well?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did Ratko Nikolic remain?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know which hospital you were taken to? Do you know the name of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I only know that at one point we were at the hospital, and it was only later on that I learnt that we were on the second floor. The window of that particular room faced the road, according to what I knew at the time. And Milomir Djukic was telling me the same. The post office was situated in that street.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall how you were transported to the hospital? Did you walk or were you taken in a vehicle; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've mentioned this several times already. I can't really remember whether we went on foot or whether they secured some sort of a truck to take us over there. I only remember that, as we arrived at the hospital, that there was a staircase there and that the soldiers assisted me to reach the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What was the physical condition of yourself and the other prisoners who were with you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in a very bad condition. We could hardly move. I think the other two also had to be assisted to reach the hospital room we were staying in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you all put in the same room with Djukic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were all staying together. But we were not being beaten there, we were not mistreated, we were not locked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to Milomir Djukic, this is the same person who had previously been -- who had been with you in the cell prior -- the one who gave you the list, you testified to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to dwell on this, Ms. Richardson. We heard it all yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, were you all put in the same room, yourself and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you receive treatment, medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I put it down in my report, I was very grateful for that. I was given some injections, pills, and this probably helped me to stay alive and live to see my exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were the other prisoners, as far as you could see, including Djukic, were they treated medically as well?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the others were also treated, including Djukic. What sort of a treatment that was, I can't tell. But they paid more attention to Djukic than to us, the nurses there. They would bring him newspapers, and he was very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was this room that you were in kept locked, and was there a guard?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the room was locked, but I'm not sure whether there was a guard or not. It was only later on, while I was still there, that I found out that only nurses were authorised to allow people into the room. And even when these people got into the room, they never beat us or anything. They would just ask us some questions. Probably they were not allowed to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you say "these people," who are you referring to? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Or, rather, I knew two of them. One of them was Enis Odzic, I believe, was his family name. But I know his name is Enis. I knew him well. And he would come often and tell me, "Ilija, do you want me to bring any food, but bear in mind that the only thing I can bring you is the soup that my wife has cooked for us. I don't have anything else." At one point he also asked me if I knew the man who had come with him, and I said that I didn't, although I did, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Where did you know this man that was with him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to finish. He told me, "How come you don't know him? He's also a neighbour of ours," my friend told me. And then this man started explaining to me, "I was in that same truck you were brought here in, and I could have killed you there or beaten you." I said, "Thank you," but I thought to myself, I know very well what sort of a man you are. You were slapping me in the face and spitting at me, but you just won't admit it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were these men, Enis, and the other men, were they dressed in civilian or military clothing?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who was beating me in the truck wore a military uniform, whereas Enis, and I remember it well, was in civilian clothes that I used to see him in even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Were you -- I'll ask another question. Withdrawn. Did there come a time when you left the hospital or were escorted out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At some point Mandza entered the room. I only found out that his name was Mandza later on, and I learnt that from hearing his soldiers addressing him by this name. And he told us, "Chetniks, you're going to be exchanged." Never for a moment did I actually believe that this was going to be an exchange. I thought that they were just going to kill us. However, it turned out to be true. They actually took us out of the hospital. We boarded a truck, and they took us in the direction of Kragljevode for an exchange. But we stopped on our way between the court and the municipality buildings, and that's where they picked up Ratko. Ratko was seated back in the -- in the back of the truck, and I was in the cabin, together with Ahmo Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did the other prisoners remain in the hospital, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, others remained in the hospital and in the cell, at least that's what Ratko told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was there anyone else in the truck besides Ratko Nikolic, with -- and I believe you said Mandza was also there, and Tihic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this not quite clearly, but there was a truck. And up front there was the driver, Zulfo, Mandza, and another person in Skelani, who used to work in the hotel there. And then there was Ahmo, I was seated next to Ahmo, and two soldiers next to me, whereas in the back of the truck, there was Ratko with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And these soldiers were armed?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you notice --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I wasn't able to see that they were armed at that point, I realised this. As we were leaving the truck in Jadar, together with Zulfo, they were all wearing camouflage and white uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you -- were you able to see if they had radios?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they did. Unfortunately, they had good weapons, they had the radios. And I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly where we were heading. I know that it was near Jadar, in the direction of Kragljevode.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was the exchange successful? Were you exchanged that day?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one other thing that I would like to say. I'm not sure whether this took place during my first or the second exchange. The truck was unable to reach Kragljevode, so it stopped at some point. And we were being assisted by soldiers again to move. And there was this young boy from Sljivica, I believe. He was travelling with his father to this village. And he told his father, "Daddy, daddy, there was a Chetnik's head stuck on a pail here," and his father told him, "You don't know what you're talking about." And we just continued moving towards Kragljevode.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you reach Kragljevode? And if so, did anything happen when you got there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we reached Kragljevode. We stayed in that area that was closer to Srebrenica, and they went off to negotiate the exchange. They said, "We are going to discuss it with the Chetniks." They moved further away from us. They crossed this hill. I don't know what the reason for that was. We stayed over there, and soldiers would approach us to mistreat us. One of them would go and fetch a knife to butcher us; another one said, "Let's take them to the post office for a heating up"; another one went to fetch an axe. So they were just simply there mistreating us, while we were waiting for the others to return. These were all -- some of those were just threats, but for some of those, they actually went and fetched a chain that was placed beneath my chin, and then they would pull by the chain, lifting me. I was unable to move; I was in a very bad condition at the time. So this man was pulling the chain, and then as he pulled away energetically, he tore the skin on my neck -- on my chin. This exchange fell through. We were returned to the same hospital room that we were in before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did there come a time that you left or you were -- someone else -- someone came to get you again to take you to another exchange attempt?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mandza was among those who returned us to the hospital. He seemed to be a leader of a sort, although I don't know what his position was. So he and at least two other soldiers returned us back to the hospital. And then after a while - I'm not really sure how much time elapsed - the second exchange took place. If I may go on with my story, telling you about the second exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, please tell us what occurred during that second exchange. And who was in the truck with you, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second exchange took place quite soon, whether perhaps a day or two later. Mandza came to our room again and said, "Chetniks, you're going for an exchange again." Basically, it was all happening the same way as it had for the first time. The only difference was that, as we were moving in the direction of Jadar, not far from Srebrenica, the truck pulled up and the driver said, "We can't go on from here because we have to put the chains on." Zulfo Tursun, who was smiling, he hugged the other men and said, "Yes, yes, let's slaughter these Chetnik shits." Ahmo Tihic, however, opposed this. Ahmo said, "Zulfo, I would be the only one entitled to say anything about this because Ilija was a neighbour of mine." And Zulfo was not really pleased with hearing Ahmo said this and said, "Ah, Ahmo is against this." And then this silence set in. They put the chains on. We resumed our journey, reached Jadar. Zulfo dismounted the truck together with his soldiers, and we continued on to Kragljevode. Let me just add this: As we were heading towards Jadar, Ahmo fetched a bag of tobacco from his pocket and he would distribute the tobacco to whoever he wanted and as much as he wanted. But he didn't give any tobacco either to Zulfo or the driver. He asked me first whether I would like to have a smoke. I refused. And then he gave some tobacco to the two soldiers, but I can't remember whether he gave any to Mandza.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And was this second attempt successful?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. Again, they left us at this mountain pass, and they went further away to negotiate. At this point I believe Ahmo said goodbye to me, but this was not to be. He returned from the negotiations, and they told us, "What can we do? The Chetniks don't want you."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you also with Ratko Nikolic at this point? You were the only two prisoners that they were trying to exchange?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know what you were being exchanged for?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you this, if you don't mind, when we go over to the third exchange, or perhaps if you want me to say that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let's talk about that third exchange. When did that happen? You were taken back to the hospital, and then there came a time that you were -- that they came for you again. Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not going over this again. Prior to this operation, we were returned to the hospital. The conditions were the same, as was the treatment. It happened soon after, a day or two perhaps. This same man, Mandza, came over to take us away. He picked me up at the hospital, they got Ratko too, and we were on our way to Kragljevode. Once we arrived, they went off to negotiate. Mandza was back at one point, and he said, "We have made contact, and you Chetniks are to be exchanged." He took us along from that place to a place near the hunting lodge, a forest-keeper's house. There was some sort of a clearing there. We stood there waiting for a while; they were probably a bit late. And at one point, Bira yelled out, he had walked to that spot, leaving the truck further away. They said that our people wanted to exchange those that they had brought over. He said, "There is no way to go on by truck, if there are any oxen around." There were two dead bodies and three people who were still alive to be exchanged. Soon after, one of these people from the opposite side came over with some oxen. He was quite apprehensive. He said, "I won't let you use my oxen." And it appeared that he wouldn't allow us to use them. At that point another man said, "Why the why are you afraid? There are five or six of. Come on, let's load those people and get back." And Bira got the leads, the chains that were attached to the oxen, and the oxen were pulling a cart. On the cart there was a coffin. They went as far as the truck and they loaded two dead bodies and two people who were still alive onto the cart. Having done that and reached us, they exchanged greetings. I remember clearly that Bira gave Mandza some sort of a box, or a carton of Drina cigarettes. They said their good-byes, and we headed back for the truck while they headed back to Srebrenica. While moving back to the exchange, where the truck was, halfway down the path, in a pine wood, suddenly there was a burst of gunfire. This was some sort of a heavy weapon, a Browning or something like that. It was strafing the trees. But the bullets were flying over our heads. They were shooting from down in the valley, probably just trying to intimidate us. I'm not sure what their intention was. Eventually we reached the truck and drove back to Jezero.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivanovic, you mentioned someone given cigarettes to Mandza during the exchange. Was this person Branislav Gligic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think I was quite clear. You have it in my description. That person was never there, and you have others to prove this. Bira was there and Cira too. That's what we used to call them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The dead bodies that were exchanged, do you know who these people were? Were they soldiers or civilian bodies; do you know? Did anyone say?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard was that one of those dead bodies, the man had been killed on the 16th when I was captured, and the man's name apparently was Beli. Probably they wanted him in exchange for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to take you back just briefly to the point where you were in the hospital. How long -- how many days did you spend in the hospital before you were actually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say quite clearly, didn't I, that I couldn't remember that. Whether it was five or six days, thereabouts, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during the time that you were in the hospital, were you able to see outside, to see events or anything that was occurring outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did say this a couple of times. I was not able to see anything because I was not able to get out of bed. But once, Miloje Djukic yelled at us, all of us who were there, not just myself, something along the lines of, "Come over and have a look. Naser and his people are getting ready to go hunting in Bratunac." He said that they were armed with snipers, that they were wearing camouflage uniforms, and they had a van that was painted in camouflage too, like their uniforms. Again, I must say I was unable to get out of bed and have a look for myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know if Milomir Djukic knew who Naser Oric was? Did he ever tell you if he knew Naser Oric before?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he knew him. Whether it was while he was there or from before is something I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have a moment. Your Honour, at this time we do have some medical documents that I'd like to have a Prosecution's exhibit placed on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are not in the record yet, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I just have a question for you before you're given the exhibits. Did you seek medical treatment after you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you recall when you were treated, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given treatment at the hospital in Bajina Basta, and the name of the nurse was Slavica Andzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you receive any other treatment? Did you visit doctors, or did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that moment on, I went to my uncle's brother's house. His name is Stanko. I spent between 10 and 15 days there. He had a heating system in place. Doctors came over to his house, and a nurse. A doctor from Belgrade came over who checked me and told me what exactly I should eat on account of my great exhaustion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And are you still getting medical treatment today for any of those injuries?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis. I have some documents with me now that I brought over from home. I used to have a lot more. I am -- I have a 40 per cent invalidity on account of the wounds that I received at the time and the bones that were broken. A lot of things were taken from me, even the original documents. I'm not even sure who took them away, without even letting me know so that I could make copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time I'd like the usher to place Prosecution Exhibit, ERN number 03639869.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the document, Mr. Ivanovic. Does this represent one of the medical records for treatment to -- for the injuries that you received during the time that you were held in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this record, one of them is dated --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several of these. I have some from the military hospital, from the military academy hospital, as well as from the Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This particular document is just one of the many medical documents you say you have as a result of where you were treated.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I stated on a number of occasions, these are not only doctors' findings and opinions as they were at the time. These problems persist, and I still have to see doctors regularly because of the difficulty that I'm experiencing. I have pain in my joints and in my bones. I found it -- I find it very difficult to move. There's a cracking sound in my knees, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are moving too slowly, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're getting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, there are two certificates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I was just going to get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not one. One refers to 1993 and to 1996. Go straight to the point, please, and whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This medical record indicates that you were treated on March 1st, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That he was examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That you were examined.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. When I was released from captivity, if I may explain, I asked my relative, my uncle's brother, not to send me to hospital. I had no idea that I would make it, that I would survive at the time. I thought I was meant to die, and I preferred to die at home. But once I recovered a little, I started visiting hospitals. There is a long list of doctors that I saw. For a long time I would go to a hospital every once in a while, and I saw a great number of doctors at the time and later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I want you, then, to go to the specifics of the report itself. But there's another report that's attached where you were treated or where you were seen by a doctor on the 23rd of April, 1996. Is this also part of your medical documentation for injuries?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I'm not going through these now, because I know that I haven't brought any documents that are not authentic. I received treatment in 1993, 1994, 1995, and onwards. I have various medical conditions that need to be treated. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what we can do at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next document here, ERN 03639855, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it's dated the 2nd of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is dated the 2nd of April, 1993. Mr. Ivanovic, look at the first part of -- the first half of this document. Do you recall being examined by a certain Dr. Ivan Zora, Zora something, Zoradic, on or around about the 2nd of April, 1993. Just say yes, not the details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you look to the second part, to the bottom part of this document, it says that you were also examined later on by Dusan -- Dr. Dusan Jandric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to the next document which bears ERN 03639856. Again, we're talking of the same Dr. Dusan Jandric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also of another doctor, Dr. Mirjana Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I may be allowed to add something in relation to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to see a rheumatology specialist and then I went to see other doctors for my other conditions, if that's of any assistance to you. I'm not sure if I should give you all the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you don't need to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to say is that this is just one specialist that I saw at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next document, 03639858, usher, please. And again, this refers to the 29th of December, 1993. You were examined -- do you recall being examined roundabout that time by a certain doctor called Radomir something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the next document, which is ERN 03639865. And again it's divided into two parts. I invite you to have a quick look at both parts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that. I know all of this by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you confirm that these are genuine documents, and they refer to examinations, medical examinations and treatment that you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are any remaining doubts, I'm sure I'm in a position to disprove them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no remaining doubts. Let's go through them now for the purpose of registration, documenting. The first document, 03639869, is being tendered and admitted as Exhibit P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, P476.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P476. The next document, bearing ERN 03639855, will be P477. The next document, bearing ERN 03639856, will be P478. The next document, bearing ERN 03639858, will be P479. And the next document, bearing ERN 03639865, will be P480. All right? Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Next I would move to a different area, of a series of exhibits. I would ask the usher's assistance in showing the witness Prosecution Exhibit 43, that's ERN -- the B/C/S 020304194, and I believe it's on Sanction. One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, can you see before you what's before you on the screen on Sanction? It's a document. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document relates to Rade Pejic. I don't see why this exhibit is being shown to this witness or how he's supposed to help with it. It's not by him. I reiterate my objection that I stated yesterday to showing this witness, of thirty exhibits which have got nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still don't know what the question is, so I will decide, or we will decide when we know what the question is. You may be right, you may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll soon see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at this point it would be easier for the witness to read from the ELMO and the hard copy. I don't know if Mr. Ivanovic can see the screen properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Are you able to read that screen properly, Mr. Ivanovic, or would you prefer the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would suggest that he is given the original in his own language, and that on the screen we see the English translation, because that's what --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We can arrange that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that's what -- I'm sure it can, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to read through this document, or just the discharge letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, I have a series of questions for you with respect to this document. If you take a look at it for a moment, this document states that it's a hospital discharge, and I'm, of course, reading from the English translation. It's in regards to Rade Pejic, and it states that he was treated from the 21st of March, 1993 until 8 May 1993. And my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question to you is whether or not Rade Pejic was, in fact, with you during the time that you were in the Srebrenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's mentioned that, he's told us that already.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll move to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But to put that question which you had already put in some 45 or one hour ago. Did you need to show him this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You asked him who was with him in the hospital and he told you. He told you all the names, the three of them, and that when they arrived there they found Milomir Djukic. So, I don't know why we need this document to prove --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just simply trying to corroborate with the document itself, since these were already tendered. And indeed, I think this is -- I think it's a relative area, highly probative, confirming what the document is and what it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's absolutely superfluous, Ms. Richardson. Let's move to more concrete matters, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I'll have the witness shown Prosecution Exhibit 44, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivanovic, this document is from --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you take a look at the document, it's from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Srebrenica armed forces, it's dated the 28th of January, from the -- to the Commission for Mediation with the enemy. And it has your name on it. My question to you: With respect to the information in this document that you were born on the 1st of February, 1961, in Cosici, the son of Radenko. Now, with respect to the basic information, can you confirm that you, in fact, did speak with individuals while you were imprisoned in Srebrenica, and that you gave them information?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this was not the case. I've not seen this document, but I can go through it, if you like. I think the data was copied from my identity card which was seized from me at the time same time my wallet was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If we can go through this and if you can tell us whether or not this was information that you gave to the individuals that you spoke to during the time that you were held in Srebrenica during the interrogation. Did you in fact advise them of your date of birth, that you were born in Cosici, that you're the son of Radenko, that you permanently reside in Bajina Basta since 1996, that you're married to Nada, and that you were employed in Belgrade. Did you give them this information?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, frankly, I don't remember. I believe they had everything on me, even what they wrote about me working at the Prajd Montaza [phoen] company. My health booklet was in my wallet. Believe me, I don't remember ever being asked this. Don't think I'm trying to fool you or anything like that. I wouldn't have a reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, we need to stop here because of technical reasons. We will have a 30-minute, full, break, and then we will resume immediately after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, prior to the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The hour that you told us you would need from today has already gone into two hours. How much longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Before the break, you were shown Prosecution Exhibit P44, and this document, it's from the armed forces to the Commission for Mediation. Do you recall during the time you were held in Srebrenica that you visited any commission that dealt with exchanges or mediation? Do you recall visiting a commission or group of people or anyone that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not receiving any interpretation, so it's quite possible that the witness isn't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we please check. Mr. Ivanovic, when Ms. Richardson was asking you a question now, were you receiving interpretation? No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I think we need to find a remedy to that. And was the accused receiving interpretation or not? Are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we have a technical problem. One moment. What I require from the technical team is an indication of whether we need to stay in the courtroom or whether you would prefer us to go out for a few minutes. All right, okay, so we'll wait here. I was so happy when you said another 10 minutes, Ms. Richardson. I will say a few words just to test the interpretation. Are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not whether you can hear me, whether you can hear the voice of the person or persons who are translating into your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the problem is not solved as yet. Do you confirm, Ms. Vidovic, because I have to rely on you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My client and I can hear the interpretation now. Now we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And again, I will repeat something just for testing whether you are receiving interpretation in your language now of what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I think we can proceed. And now you have three minutes less, Ms. Richardson. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, before the break you were shown Prosecution Exhibit P44, and it is -- it states on this document that recommendations were made with respect to a Commission for Mediation. Did you visit at any time, or were you taken to any commission that dealt with exchanges during the time that you were held in the prison?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were any of the other prisoners taken to any commission, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Also, with respect to a high court, were you taken to any high court for adjudication or questioned, or were any of the other prisoners, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was only taken to this person in the municipality building. I don't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I'd ask that Prosecution Exhibit 48 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask if you recall -- this is, again, a document from the Srebrenica armed forces to the Commission for Mediation to the enemy, and it's dated 31st of January, 1993.
