This is in respect to Milisav Milovanovic, son of Rade. Do you know if this person is or do you know if this is the Mico you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, if we have the same person in mind, Rade, who I was talking about, also known as Kojo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And he was from Sase?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Sase. Milisav, Mico. If you're referring to Mico from Sase, that's how I remembered him and wrote his name down, after captivity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 50, 5-0.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This document is a war -- is entitled "War Hospital Srebrenica, Forensic Report," it's in regard to Milisav Milovanovic, born in 1950. And just the second paragraph, it states: "A medical examination was performed on the 12th of February." In addition to that information, it also states that he was given medical assistance and kept in the hospital. "Due to lack of proper medication and seriousness of illness, the above named died on the same day." It also states further down, the last sentence: "Based on the information provided by the patient that day, as well as external examination, no traces of violence or injuries were detected." Now, Mr. Ivanovic, I draw your attention to when Mico died in the prison. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well when it was that Mico died. Now, as for the information contained herein, somebody must have tried to present things the way they wanted, because as far as I know, Mico was never taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did he receive any medical treatment in the prison, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And on the day he died, or prior to his death, was he beaten, and did he have physical injuries?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now I would ask the --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. One day, before he passed away, a young man came, as I've already told you, and beat him in the chest. The following morning, Ratko told us that Mico had already died and probably as a result of injuries sustained in the beating by this young man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I'd ask the usher's assistance to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I'd ask the usher's assistance and present document P53 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This is a document that's entitled "Srebrenica War Hospital, record of on-site Investigation of Death." It states: "On the 19th of March, 1993 the death of the above-named man was established. He was undergoing medical treatment until March 3rd 1993. He died on 19th March 1993 on prison premises." Further down, the last sentence reads: "No traces of injuries or violence found on the body." Now, Mr. Ivanovic, the last time you saw Branko Sekulic was where?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Branko Sekulic the last time when I was taken to the hospital, and I remember very well the condition he was in when I left, and his condition was a result of the beatings. And I claim with certainty that nobody ever came to provide any medical treatment to him or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 68.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This is a Srebrenica War Hospital, a record of on-site investigation of death, and this is in regards to Dragan Ilic. It states that it was the death of the aforementioned was established on the 10th of March, 1993. He underwent hospital treatment until 3rd of March, 1993. And finally, there were no signs of injuries or violence on the body. Now, the last time -- could you tell us, when was the last time you saw Dragan Ilic, and what was his physical condition?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't want to -- I don't know what to say to this. I keep telling you that there was no medical assistance, that we were beaten up, done in, I don't know how to put it. They're mentioning medical assistance here, but I can tell you that there was none of that, except for the treatment I underwent at the hospital. So that's what I can tell you, aside from just looking at the document and the name on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So the last time you saw Dragan Ilic, he was in the prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it appeared as though he had been beaten up?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all lying around, and they were basically dead people, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And is that the same for Djukic, Jakov? You can just answer with a verbal yes.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the last time you saw Milomir Djukic was in the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what condition was he in?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this several times, that it was such a pity for him to actually have been treated well and recovered, I mean his legs, and then to have probably died, at least that's what I think, because he never went back home again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, I would like Prosecution Exhibit P4 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: The witness said not to have probably died but to have probably been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time I'd like the usher's assistance in showing the witness Prosecution Exhibit 458, and specifically if you could assist with locating page 47 of the B/C/S, ERN number 03593170. In the English version of this document, the information is located on page 31. The page number is at the top. It's handwritten. The English is not on Sanction. Right now we have the B/C/S on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, if you -- can you take a look at that document and tell the Trial Chamber whether you recognise anyone from -- that's listed in that document. Maybe I can assist, Your Honour in light of the time.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise Kostadin Popovic as someone who was with you in the prison?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Milomir Djukic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ratko Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's page, of the English version --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I see you're listed here as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And there is also -- do you see anyone else that you recognise on that page? Milenko Trifunovic? Maybe it's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he's on the other page, Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before I start, Your Honour, just to make clear that we obviously -- we have objected to all the exhibits that have been shown, and particularly also this diary which was found in a meadow, or whatever the evidence was. We strongly object to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I may, for the record, just state something with respect to this exhibit, specifically 458. It was presented by Nikola Popovic, as you recalled. He has contacted our office. He said that he located the copy of the document, and we're making arrangements at this moment to have it submitted to the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Now, before you start your cross-examination, Mr. Jones, just some housekeeping matters. Today is Tuesday. It's obvious that we are not going to finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was Your Honour addressing me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's obvious we're not going to finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, just to put this in context, the original estimate given by the Prosecution was three hours for this witness. We've gone past the six-hour mark. And I actually do want to make a point about that, that for our preparation never mind the Victims and Witnesses Unit, never mind the Bench, it's not helpful to have such unrealistic time estimates, and it means I have to revise my estimate, because obviously the witness has given a lot more evidence than I expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, with the important, or more important witnesses, I have already made the Trial Chamber's position clear, and there will we no restrictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, so three and a half hours, I would say, at this point, is my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need three and a half hours, which basically leaves us with one hour now, and then we need another two and a half hours tomorrow, which would then, more or less, leave us with one hour for the next witness, number 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twenty-six. And witness 26, who will be dealing with that witness? Madam Vidovic, how much time do you think you will require for that witness. The Prosecution is saying one hour, but that is, again, very conservative, according to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the examination-in-chief will remain within the ambit of what the witness had stated to the OTP, I believe that the cross-examination will last some 45 minutes to one hour at most. But it seems to be customary with the OTP to include some facts other than those contained in the statement, and if that will be the case, then my examination will probably last longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can say with some certainty that this estimation is correct for the next two witnesses, 26 and 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the 26, you need one hour, and the Defence will need one hour, so basically that could cover the next witness -- the next witness, one hour and one hour. And the other one, 27, you say one hour, but then you indicate two days, 26 and 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that that was indicated only if this person ran out of time and this person would have gone into the next day. So I think it was estimated based on this witness finishing Wednesday, the next one, Djukic, starting on Thursday, and then number 27 starting and then finishing the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. This witness will finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Right, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will be roughly two hours -- two and a half hours into tomorrow, so it will be the first break plus halfway, serious halfway, into the second session. Roughly I consider that we will only be left with one hour for the next witness, and that will be tomorrow, Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And we can conduct the direct examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, which basically brings us into Thursday, and Defence will need another hour to finish that witness off, okay? Then we have the other witness, and you say one hour. And the Defence, with regard to witness 27?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in relation to witness 27, we will be requiring at least one hour, perhaps even as much as one hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, because Thursday we have to stop at 12, maximum 12.30, but certainly not beyond that, because one of us needs to travel, which would leave us one hour for the first witness, then another -- 9 to 10, then you have half an hour and you have an hour and a half, two hours -- two hours. I don't yet know the areas that witness 27 will touch. But what I want to avoid is have witness 27 stay over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that these last two witnesses for the week are witnesses who will be confirming the deaths of relatives, and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So take it for granted that, with regard to those two witnesses, 26, 27, we will be imposing a time limit, okay? And make sure that we will finish with both by the end of -- by the end of the second session on Thursday, on Thursday. All right. Yes. Now, Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Jones begins, and I don't want to necessarily discuss this in front of the witness, but we haven't received an exhibit list. Is it that the witness doesn't have one for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I mean, it's standard practice on our side, that if we're going to use prior witness statements, that we don't specifically notify those, and that's been a practice which the Prosecution has accepted. So I don't preclude that we will use prior statements, but no exhibits beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ivanovic, Mr. Jones will be asking you some questions, and I would like to remind you of my words of last week I think it was, or last Monday, that you are compelled to answer all his questions truthfully and fully, in the same manner you have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecutor. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to start by taking you right back to the beginning and to the area of Cosici, which I imagine you know very well.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just to help us get our bearings, you said that Cosici is in a valley. Is there a river running through Cosici?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Does that river flow down to the Drina?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that the route that civilians took on the 16th of January, 1993 when they went towards Bajina Basta? Did they go along the river?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, not up the river but rather down the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. But did they follow the river down to or up to Skelani and Bajina Basta? Is that the route they took?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those that I know of at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So could you tell us what route they did take on that day?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least that time, I know because of my mother who I was with in the village at that time, they went via Maltasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that they went between the villages of Tihic and Malta?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found out later, because I didn't follow them, one group went via Tihici, and another group, when they met the Muslim forces, just scattered. That's what they told me and what my mother told me. Some of them crossed over in that area. I can't tell you where to exactly. But I know that they were moving towards Maltasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll come back to that in a moment with a map. First, I want to ask you some questions about 1992, so even before the attack of the 16th of January. Now, you told us you came from Serbia to defend your home village of Cosici. Can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, specifically, the first thing I want to say is that I first came -- I had worked in Montenegro, in a town called Tivat, for a military company. When I arrived from there, it was for a feast day of St. Lazarus. As usual, we held the ceremony, and from that time to the day I was captured, I spent between 80 and 90 per cent of my time in Bajina Basta with my wife, my brother, my sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, Mr. Ivanovic, just so we can take these points quickly. Is there a date, even an approximate date, of when you went and joined what you called the village guard in Cosici?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We joined this village guard in the most serious fashion after Christmas fell. When it had all burned down, we took a very serious approach to defending our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you talking about Christmas 1993, orthodox Christmas? I'm simply not following you. When did you join the village guard in Cosici, where you found yourself on the 16th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to come and see my mother on a regular basis, to our home. We had some land there which we worked. At the time the house I had in Bajina Basta was something that I did not consider a home. My home was in Cosici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. So when did you move over to Cosici?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Cosici, I've said this, and I will say it again, we seriously joined the village guard after Bozici had burned down. I had been in Bajina Basta at the time, staying with my wife's brother, and I actually saw the village burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right, then, that from the 7th of January, 1993, to the 16th of January, 1993, only, that that was the period that you were in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before that time, but not that seriously, really, which means whenever we came, we had some sort of a guard with less people. It was some sort of a patrol. I'm not sure what I should call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I take it, then, that you never engaged in combat action in other villages or hamlets in this area before the 16th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Never. I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You hadn't seen any combat action whatsoever until that date?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I said I'd go back to the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was going to use P472, but it actually appears to be two maps stuck together. It's something we can see later. But I prefer to use this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out because it was not pointed out before, although we noticed it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to use copies of this map instead, which is one which we have. There should be one for the witness and one for each of Your Honours, and one for the Prosecution, of course. Do we have enough? Otherwise I can put my copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we all have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm happy to offer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's enough, actually, because the witness won't be needing it after he's finished with it. So we have enough, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'll have to ask you, first of all, to mark Cosici on that map. I hope it won't be too problematic. You can see Bozici, which I've highlighted, and even the most approximate mark where Cosici is would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could just put a square for Cosici.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now could you mark the escape route, which you mentioned earlier, which civilians took when they left Cosici to get to Bajina Basta. Again, just approximately.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could mark it with a pen.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But from Cosici, how did they get to Malta? If you could just mark that as well.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I can't see Cosici clearly enough on the map in order to be able to mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Ivanovic, you recall that a couple of minutes ago you put a small circle near Pavkovici, and we took it that you were indicating for us Cosici, because the question that had been put to you before was precisely to show us on the map where you think Cosici was. So if you want to revise that, you can revise it. I can tell you that the point which you indicated today does not correspond with the point that you indicated yesterday. Yesterday you said that it was between Bozici and Kolari.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I got it wrong, but believe me, I do know the area well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For my purposes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the witness should, I imagine, initial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the registrar is right, because on that document, you can barely distinguish the lines that he has drawn. So I would suggest that if you have another spare copy which you can let us have, Mr. Jones -- or we can use the same one -- but I can ask him to draw the lines again in red, or some other colour, which will --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With a highlighter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's too big. That's too big. Yes, give him -- okay, give him that. At least it's of a different colour anyway. Okay. The red one is okay. The red one is okay. So you need to redraw in red the two routes, the one from Skelani and the one from Cosici. The one from Cosici to Malta, and the one from Skelani ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then from, basically, Pavkovici to Cosici, if you could just show where the civilians would have gone to get from Cosici to Pavkovici, on that map.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two villages that are nearly one village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You think that Cosici is practically in Pavkovici?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The two villages that are connected, forming almost one village. Between the two villages, there is a single house midway between the two, which is no distance at all, really. I think you'd be perfectly right calling it one village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. That's helpful. I think you still need to initial the line that you have drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you put your initials at the beginning and at the end of those lines, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, sticking with that map for a little bit longer, do you see Daljegosta on the map? Or, indeed, are you familiar with Daljegosta?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that that's just a few kilometres away from Cosici?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The distance between Daljegosta and Cosici, if you have that in mind. I'm not sure which one's Mala and which one's Velika because there are two. If you mean the one with the mosque, in that case, I can tell you my assessment of the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've mentioned a mosque. So is it right that that was a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's Velika or Mala or both?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I think that there was a place called Velika and a place called Mala Daljegosta.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Ismet Hodzic or Odzic. He was from Daljegosta, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Arapovici, should I say, or Jezce. Maybe you could call it Jezce, but I think it was from Arapovici. He is a shop owner, and that's how I know. I'm certain about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you saw him later in Srebrenica. When you saw him --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- when you saw him, didn't he tell you that your father, Radenko, had saved him in some way?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. I think it happened in the prison. Once he barged in, saying something like, "Ilija, thank you so much. Your father helped me to save my life."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't your father advise Ismet at the start of the war that he should move his family from the village? Isn't that how he --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it might as well have been that. Maybe he told him something, but I wasn't there when they talked and when he told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Ismet did move his family away from the area, didn't he? But he himself went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. He even once told me their whereabouts. That was during my captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the Serbs, like your father Radenko, stayed in the villages in your area, but the Muslims left; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My father, Radenko, left later. I had begun to build a house upon my return from Libya. I returned back in 1986. I only had one small bit that was finished, where my brother and his wife lived, and he wanted to have at least another section built, because up to that point, they'd only had one small room.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, Mr. Ivanovic, because you're giving a lot of detail, and it may mean that we stay here longer than we need to. I'll ask very short questions, and you can usually provide a short answer. My question, really, was this: Isn't it right that the Muslims in this whole area, this broader area, were leaving in 1992 because they didn't feel safe there anymore?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. To the best of my recollection, they were leaving, and they were probably seen out with dignity. I would like you to prove that anyone was even cocked as new cats on their way out to Serbia. I was in the village and I should know, but I wish I hadn't been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you were in the village in 1992, there in Cosici?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this before, and I'll repeat it for you: I would come to Cosici every once in a while. It's my village. That is why I can be sure about the things I'm telling you. As for when exactly I came, I really can't be sure, because I would come and go. After Bozici fell, I spent most of my time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That might be the confusion earlier when you were referring to Bozic and Bozici. It's a town, not just a date. Leaving that to one side. You also mentioned Ahmo Tihic yesterday, and today indeed. He's the brother of Dzemo Tihic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's a town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm asking about the person Ahmo Tihic. He's the brother of Dzemo Tihic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Which village was he from?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tihic? Tihic, Lijesce. I'm not sure what else to call it. I know where his house used to be, his shop. I know his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you saw him in Srebrenica. Isn't that because he, too, had to leave Tihici and go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he left for Srebrenica, but I did see him over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You saw these villages, you explained how you're familiar with the area. By January the 16th, 1993, there were no Muslims in Tihici, were there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Nor were there Muslims in Arapovici at that moment.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In Dobrak.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't go into that. That wasn't near where I was. I will tell you whatever I can, but I did say a while ago that I spent quite little time in the area, because previously I had worked for a company in Belgrade and also abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So just sticking with the area that you know, isn't it right to summarise that, by the 16th of January, 1993, there were no Muslims in that area?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the area through which I was passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And those people, then, having left their houses, that would be, would it not, a lot of Muslim men, women, and children who would have left their homes; hundreds, perhaps thousands even. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Probably. I don't know the number, but they did leave, that's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see the woods from Cosici? And if you could, did you not see flames and fires there, of people, Muslims, living in the woods?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were Muslims living in the woods in makeshift shelters?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. It was proven that they were there throughout the area, as far as Skelani, as far as the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, your area was part of Srebrenica municipality before the war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then when the war started, our sometime in 1992, it became a new municipality of Skelani, didn't it, if you're aware.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, the exact area under the municipality. I didn't spend that much time thinking about it. I thought more about my own village, as well as the house that I owned over in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But the picture I'm painting for you and which I'm going to suggest to you now is that, what was happening in your area is that Serbs were expelling all the Muslims so that that area, the new municipality of Skelani, could become annexed to Serbia as part of a greater Serbia. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can shed any light on that. I only know that, whenever I came to my village, I could notice, on the Muslim houses, for example, that they were marked. There were planks on their roofs. That's the sort of thing they had. I have no idea what that was supposed to mean, though. As for this greater Serbia, it's something that you're now telling me about. For me, Serbia is when I come home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But you came from Serbia to fight in Cosici, didn't you? Did you see part of your fight as being to keep that area within the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could answer first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness answer the question first, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean, from Serbia? I was just coming home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In any event, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My objection was the way the question was phrased, which I think he asked the witness if he came to fight. I don't think he testified he came to fight. I think he came to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it was a suggestion that was being put to him, and I think he has answered both.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe just one more question on that point. At this time did you see home, Cosici, and Serbia, Bajina Basta, as being one country?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. As regards that, the answer is no. I grew up, after all, in Bosnia-Herzegovina in my home, and I am still very much a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I own this other house in Bajina Basta, believe me that this is still the village that I go to very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand that. Now, have you heard of the expression "torbari"? Does it mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know what that might mean, torbar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, you told us yesterday that how from Maltaska Gradina, when you were up there, you saw "an enormous column" of Muslim men, women, and children stretching a kilometre from the direction of Colakovici. Now, stopping there for a moment --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colavici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Colavici, okay. Now, this column stretching a kilometre long, would you agree that that would have been composed of thousands of people?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I saw thousands of people. And it's not from Maltasi that I saw them. I saw them as I was moving away from Maltasi. And I really can't say how distant I was from the column when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that there were hundreds of people in the column?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. There were many people there in one column that must have been stretching for at least one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were interviewed about this in 2002, you stated, and I'll -- I don't need to show you this statement, I'll just read it for you. But the reference for us is page 3 of that statement, and it's ERN 01171375, paragraph 16. But there, speaking of the same events, you said: "They were coming from all over. Ninety per cent of them were young. Some were young men, some were young girls." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps something there was altered in my statement, because I don't agree with everything in relation to the army. As for the people arriving from Colakovici, I wouldn't agree with that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were speaking earlier about people coming from Colakovici. In fact, the location isn't really important. Do you agree that there were many young people in the column, firstly?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were also young people there, and I said that there were women, children, men. They had horses with them as well. And they were banging on some containers. Probably their intention was to make a lot of noise. That's what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm coming to that, and there's no need to repeat what you've said already. We do have a record. What I wanted to ask you was, did you see that many of these people were carrying bags to put food in?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my vantage point, from the distance I was at, I was unable to see any bags. I told you that I did see the column. And there were many horse-drawn carts in the column as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Horses in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just sticking with the women, for a moment, who you saw, I want to clarify a matter you spoke about yesterday. It seemed that you were suggesting that every single girl or woman had an automatic rifle. I'll read what you said, and then you can say whether that's correct or not. And the reference is page 21 of the transcript yesterday, lines 5 to 17. "Q. What were the approximate ages of girls you described in uniforms or partial uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from 17 to 20 years of age. Perhaps some of them were younger." Skipping a bit. "Q. And were they also carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. All of them had weapons of much better quality than we did. All of them were automatic weapons." So I just want to check that. Do you wish to correct that, or do you maintain that every single woman or girl which you saw that day was in a camouflage uniform and had an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing for me to correct there. I said that that I was describing the group that I came across and that captured me. I wasn't describing the group that was moving from the direction of Colakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify that matter. Now, staying with the column and the people you saw in the column, and the banging of pots which you described, could you agree that this was a scene of complete chaos, with all these civilians running all over the place?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they were after, but I know that first there would be the army seizing the area, then there would be others looting belongings and taking them away. And I don't know what else I can say to explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to say, for the civilians, then, no one appeared to be in control of them, and no one could control them; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell, really. Whether they had a leader or not, I don't know. But I know that I saw the column of people, but I did not see them arriving in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On that day you recognised many people as local Muslims, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right, then, that possibly many of them, many of the Muslims you saw, were Muslims who had left their homes in the area earlier and were now coming back?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among those who attacked my village, I could not recognise a single person. But as they were coming into the village, I could recognise some persons. And it's good of you to have reminded me. The password was Naser Gada, and I was able to see quite clearly what clothes they wore and what weapons they carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't see how I reminded you of that password, but we'll move on from there. Would you agree, from the way you were treated when you were immediately arrested, that local Muslims were very angry at the Serbs, at people they saw as local Serbs, because of what had passed, because of them having to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were angry or not. I repeat: Those of us who were there were in our own homes. I have to tell you that 12 people got killed there, after all. Now, angry or not, they did come to my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. As I say, there's no need to repeat matters you've already dealt with, and you did tell us that yesterday. And since you raise the matter of the-- guarding your homes, I'm going to move to another set of questions, and I'm going to come back to what we were discussing earlier. You've told us that you were simply a member of the village guard, and that the Serb army didn't give you help of any kind; is that right? No instructions or anything.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I'm telling you now that whenever I went to the village, I'd always get something, a rifle or something else, to stand guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wasn't there a Skelani battalion at that time, and weren't you part of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Skelani battalion was not there with us, and you can easily check that, that is, you can easily infer that from the number of people who got killed there, the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's take -- let's just stick with you. You were in full camouflage uniform on the 16th of January, 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that, as you said in your 2002 statement, "I was wearing a camouflage jacket, camouflage trousers, and boots. I carried my automatic rifle." Do you agree with all of that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not wish to deny that. I want to say something that I've already emphasised earlier on: I went to the village to help my neighbours and relatives. Whenever I did go there, I put on whatever clothes I had. Whether they were civilian clothes or a camouflage uniform, I did not pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, as I've said, you have dealt with a lot of these areas before. I'm going to ask you very specific questions, and I would appreciate it if you would simply answer yes or no, if you can. Now, on that day, didn't you also have grenades, or at least a grenade?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. This is what we call in English a grenade. You pull a pin out, and then throw it, and it explodes. That's what you had.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, what --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I've described that several times already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were all 25 of you, in what you called the village guard, issued with grenades, or was it just you, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was by coincidence. Whatever we had here at hand at the time of the start of the attack, whatever we did have at our disposal, we used. I wish to repeat that that very night I was asleep because I was not standing guard that morning, just prior to the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that you were sleeping at your mother's house, and that you woke at 5.45 a.m. So is it right, then, that sleeping at your mother's house, you were in that full regalia, camouflage jacket, camouflage trousers, boots, machine-gun and grenades. You had all of that with you when you were sleeping at your mother's.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had those clothes, and I must have had the rifle, or rather, I've explained this several times, I had a PAP, semi-automatic rifle. And when my cousin, my uncle's son, got killed, I took his automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You spoke about that yesterday. I thought your evidence was that the Muslims left your cousin's rifle, but in fact you tell us now that you took it.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of having said that, because this cousin of mine, my uncle's son, got killed while we were pulling out, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can read it back to you.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was at page 21 of the transcript, lines 13 to 17: "Let me explain to you. When my cousin was killed, he was wearing" - that's what it says - "a semi-automatic rifle, and as they killed him, they just left the rifle standing there. They refused to take it with them, so you can imagine what sort of weaponry they had." Wasn't that your evidence, that the Muslims left the rifle after they had killed him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that this is some sort of a misunderstanding, because this particular rifle belonged to my relative who got killed at Maltaska Gradina and not to my cousin, who was shot by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's take that, then. You say, if that's your cousin, that's the one who blew himself up with the grenade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You told us that your cousin Mile accidentally or on purpose detonated a grenade and killed himself. Isn't that the cousin you're talking about on Maltaska Gradina?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this did not take place in the village you have asked me about. I know what I said and what I experienced. What you were talking about now relates to my relative Mile who got killed at Maltaska Gradina. We found this shelter in a ditch next to the road, and my relative was lying prone -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll stop you. You don't need to --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain it to you in detail, but you must have misunderstood this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've explained this before. My point to you now is this: If, when you were talking about your cousin Mile, you were talking about the person who blew himself up, then why did you say, "when my cousin was killed, he was wearing a semi-automatic rifle, and as they killed them, they just left the rifle standing there"? The Muslims didn't kill them, did they? He killed himself.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several of my relatives there, and I have to tell you that I took the rifle off my relative -- off my cousin who was shot by a sniper in the village, as we were pulling out in the direction of Maltasi. And I don't really understand how it was possible for you to skip this part about the village and turn to Maltasi and my relative and his rifle there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivanovic, please don't argue with Mr. Jones. He is doing his duty. He has a right to ask you questions. If you don't agree with what he's putting to you, just answer yes or no, or give reasons why you don't agree. But you don't enter into a direct confrontation with him. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And my point is this, Mr. Ivanovic, and I'm not going to dwell on it: But weren't you suggesting yesterday that Mile had been killed by the Muslims when you said that, "as they killed him," when you know full them that no one killed him, he killed himself.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I did say that he killed himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's go back to the village guard. You said also that you later got a mortar. Now, when was that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point I was not in the village. On one occasion, when I went there, just immediately prior to the attack, I was at my home in Bajina Basta. I think I've described this already. This cousin of mine, who was due to have his baby, he told me, "Cousin, don't leave, because Sladza is about to give birth." And I said I had to go --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question was nothing of that sort. My question was: When did the village guard get the mortar? It's a very simple question, if you could please answer it.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you, because at that point I was in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've accepted that you were in a full camouflage uniform on the 16th of January, 1993, that you had a machine-gun and grenades. Who supplied you with all those things, if not the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much about this. I repeat that I would often go to Bajina Basta, and then upon my return, whatever weaponry we had, we used for our defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So, in fact, you can't say for sure who supplied the village with those things. You can't say that it wasn't the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yesterday you were pretty categorical that it wasn't the Serb army, and that's why I'm clarifying it. So do you say that you were not a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the Serbian army did that. But if -- if time allowing, I would like to explain this to you in more detail. As I was going over there to defend the village, I was probably -- I would probably, as such, classify as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, in fact, when you were brought to Srebrenica, you had a military identification booklet on you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Doesn't that mean that you were a soldier in the Serb army on the 16th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, because this military booklet dated from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. There's a medical certificate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a second here. Was it a JNA military booklet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On the subject of grenades, isn't it right that after Mile detonated his grenade, that you dropped yours and then you couldn't find it among the leaves?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't throw it away. While Mile Ivanovic's grenade went off - and in this explosion, my hand and my leg were injured - in this process, with the blast, my grenade simply fell and I was unable to restore it, to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. There might have been a problem in interpretation. That was all I wanted to establish, that you dropped your grenade and then you couldn't find it among the leaves. It's that specific detail which I'm asking you, if that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to answer it, because you have already answered it. Let's move to the next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It will become apparent in due course why I seek that specific detail. That's fine. We have it, we have the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us how you laid land-mines around Cosici, and in your statement of 2002, you said they were placed around three sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my memory serves me, I think I kept saying that we laid the mines in the direction from which we expected them to come. I don't know if they had been laid earlier on as well, but I do remember that after the torching of Bozici, mines were laid. Perhaps even earlier on. But you have to believe me when I tell you that I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was looking at your 2002 statement, page 2. You don't need to refer to it, but it's for the record, ERN 01171374, paragraph 7: "Land-mines were placed around three sides of the perimeter of my village of Cosici." So could that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that they were placed, but I'm not sure about the dates. I told you when I think that they were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, your average farmer wouldn't have a clue how to lay land-mines without killing or injuring himself, would he?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. But I myself did not lay these mines, nor was I aware of how that is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yesterday you were very clear that the village guard had received no instructions from the Serb army. Do you agree that actually laying land-mines, there would need to be instruction from military experts, more specifically from the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything on this matter. I know that the mines were laid by a man from this, what do you call it, defence, who had some previous experience from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you knew, in your village, didn't you, where you laid your land-mines. You kept records so that you wouldn't wander into them yourself. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I heard about that too. I told you that mines were laid in three different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So on the 16th of January, 1993, when you said you heard mines detonating, that was, in all probability, an unsuspecting Muslim who had got blown up, isn't it, rather than a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything like that. I don't remember that anything like that was ever said. I know that on the 16th, when the first mine went off, we all jumped to our feet. And one of my cousins told me, "Get up, all of you, it seems we're under attack." We headed that way to see for ourselves, because we had noticed Muslim soldiers moving along.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is my last question on this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time, at your convenience, between now and a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I had one more question, perhaps to make best use of the time, I would go a bit longer in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not beyond 1.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It would be best that I conclude this area, and then we can break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know of no instances, then, where Muslims were injured by land-mines in Cosici? Specific instances.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or where Muslims were wounded by any means in Cosici?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know how Mehmedalija Tihic came to be wounded in Cosici?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mehmedalija Tihic stepped on a mine on the road to Kolari. He was taken to Skelani to receive treatment in the presence of Mico Trifunovic. That's as much as I know. That's where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you don't know whether he survived, do you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that's probably a good moment to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I think we are moving. The only thing I wanted to ask you, Mr. Jones, is this map that you made use of in the initial period of your cross-examination, whether you want to tender it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, please. Since the witness has marked it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So this will be Defence Exhibit D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 168, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of January, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
